name: Synthetic Populations for Policy Analysis
title: Synthetic Populations for Policy Analysis
answer: Synthetic populations are artificial datasets of individuals, households, or firms designed to mirror the statistical properties of a real population while containing no actual personal records. In macroeconomic econometrics and policy analysis, they let analysts test tax, transfer, labor, and health policies on a simulated society before implementation. The scope covers generating demographic, income, employment, and geographic attributes, then using those units in microsimulation or agent-based models to estimate aggregate effects. This sits within the AI economist toolkit because modern generation methods use machine learning to capture complex dependencies that older sampling and reweighting could not.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Synthetic populations are artificial datasets of individuals, households, or firms designed to mirror the statistical properties of a real population while containing no actual personal records. In macroeconomic econometrics and policy analysis, they let analysts test tax, transfer, labor, and health policies on a simulated society before implementation. The scope covers generating demographic, income, employment, and geographic attributes, then using those units in microsimulation or agent-based models to estimate aggregate effects. This sits within the AI economist toolkit because modern generation methods use machine learning to capture complex dependencies that older sampling and reweighting could not.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard statistical and scientific computing stacks, often Python or R, with heavy use of libraries for data manipulation, optimization, and probabilistic modeling. Large synthetic populations may require distributed processing or GPU acceleration when fitting deep generative models such as variational autoencoders or normalizing flows. Storage is usually tabular or columnar, and the generated population is consumed by downstream simulation code rather than served in real time. No special hardware is required for smaller regional populations, but national-scale runs with millions of agents benefit from cloud compute.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical workflow starts with a survey or administrative microdata sample, from which a generative model learns the joint distribution of attributes. The model then draws new records, often conditioned on aggregate targets from censuses or national accounts, so the synthetic population matches known margins. Analysts validate the output by comparing distributions, correlations, and policy-relevant moments against held-out data. The synthetic population then feeds a microsimulation or agent-based model where each unit responds to policy rules, and the results are aggregated to estimate fiscal cost, inequality, or labor supply effects.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because synthetic records are not real people, privacy risk is lower than with raw microdata, but re-identification and attribute disclosure remain concerns if the generator memorizes rare combinations. Governance focuses on measuring the privacy loss of the generative model, setting disclosure thresholds, and documenting the provenance of training data and model versions. Policy analyses using synthetic populations should state clearly that results are model-dependent and not direct measurements. Rights and risk also include the possibility that biased training data produce synthetic populations that underrepresent vulnerable groups, which can distort policy conclusions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter integration of generative models with causal inference and equilibrium simulation, so synthetic populations can support counterfactual policy evaluation under less restrictive assumptions. Researchers are working on methods that preserve longitudinal and network structure, not just cross-sectional attributes, which would improve analysis of dynamic policies like pensions or unemployment insurance. There is also movement toward standardized benchmarks and open synthetic populations for reproducibility. Over time, these tools may become routine inputs to fiscal agencies and central banks, though human review of model assumptions will remain necessary.
